Hardmeier explains the anniversary volume and an institutional transition after 1989, including Willi’s new chair.
The collections combine natural history, ethnography, archaeology, literature, music and thousands of glass photographs; Neumann’s image database is a new project.
Hardmeier places Dalman’s empirical biblical context work within his theology and identifies Lehrkurse and Jewish literature as parts of the same programme.
Specialized modern disciplines limit replication of Dalman’s universal scholarship, while individual prewar objects remain historical sources requiring preservation.

Zobel opens the institutional history by describing Greifswald’s teaching collections and Koeppel relief maps; the Siloam squeeze is singled out.
The Siloam squeeze and a 1935 Dalman portrait introduce his works; Rengstorf returned material for the unfinished eighth Arbeit und Sitte volume.
Zobel describes the scale of Arbeit und Sitte and Dalman’s Moravian upbringing, name change, qualifications and early missionary ambition.
The 1899–1900 journey and Palestinian Diwan shifted his work toward field observation; the Jerusalem institute foundation deed is dated 19 June 1900.
The 1898 church dedication preceded the foundation; Dalman accepted in May 1902, arrived that autumn and opened the Jerusalem institute in November 1903.
The institute’s brief joined scholarly study and church interests; its work was independent of excavation and included natural history, antiquities, language and everyday practice.
Jerusalem’s library and museum expanded rapidly; Lehrkurse began in October 1903 and used riding excursions and extended tent journeys.
Zobel treats contemporary observation as a route into the past and lists successive Jerusalem directors; wartime separation brought Dalman to Greifswald in October 1917.
Photographs and manuscripts were shipped from Jerusalem; Greifswald obtained further collections and a substantial mixed photo archive including military aerials.
Glass positives were arranged by place and subject; Zobel’s account of demographic and cultural changes is his contextual argument for the archive’s value.
An Israeli request for copies in the mid-1970 s triggered tighter university security; resources and DDR isolation restricted access until projects began after 1989.

Männchen introduces Dalman’s appointment and his Moravian education, teaching and departure for Leipzig’s Institutum Judaicum.
His early publications addressed Judaism, anti-Jewish accusations, missionary training, messianic ideas and Aramaic philology.
The Leipzig stipend enabled the 1899–1900 trip; the institute’s assignment explicitly excluded excavation and prioritized broad local study for theological students.
Lehrkurse combined lectures, short trips and a tent journey; the early museum held archaeological, ethnographic and natural-history teaching material.
Collections grew through purchases and gifts, including DPV ceramics, architectural models and birds; Greifswald authorization followed financial provision in January 1920.
Objects transferred in 1922 acquired dedicated rooms by 1926 after a 1925 fundraising effort; Dalman described minerals, herbarium, woods and agricultural products.
Gifts came from Duncan’s City of David work, Bade’s Mizpah work, Sellin’s Shechem work and Dormition excavations; the faculty moved in 1929.
Männchen argues that small ethnographic holdings belong to Dalman’s integrated conception; a 1918 faculty letter supplies his five-part definition of the discipline.
The 1918 definition connects the five branches with modern Palestine and Jewish written sources; later reference works narrowed the discipline toward archaeology.
Männchen critiques encyclopaedic accounts that omit Dalman and his institute and detach Palestine studies from theology.
Dalman treated local knowledge as necessary to understand assumptions in biblical texts, while the Bible was itself a Palestinian product.
His geography of Jesus emphasized the whole landscape and relationships between places rather than isolated named biblical locations.
Theological election of the land connected Old and New Testaments in Dalman’s account; he opposed reducing revelation to comparative religious history.
Männchen relates his rejection of pan-Babylonian and myth theories to his programme for unified biblical languages, context and theological teaching.
Only lecture titles survive; manuscripts and student notes are absent; his final teaching in 1938 and Arbeit und Sitte close the account.

Willi introduces the Judaica room and documents the 1946 rename through UAG R 203, along with the 1920 authorization.
Willi proposes a Leipzig nucleus for the Judaica collection and possible Kahane connections; his note records the 1925 foundation’s purchase purpose.
The library preserves rare early printings and supports the new 1994 chair; Wolff’s 1993 survey supplies dated title totals.
Willi argues for reconnecting Old Testament study with Jewish reception and introduces Renaissance and Baroque engagements with Jewish sources.
Reuchlin’s defence of Hebrew and Jewish literature is considered through Herder’s retrospective account.
Bomberg’s Venetian printing is represented by Kimchi and parts of the first Babylonian Talmud; bibliographic notes explain early Christian and Jewish transmission.
Talmud page conventions derive from early printings; Constantinople Midrash editions record Sephardic printing after expulsion, with Greifswald shelfmarks.
Pesaro Megillot and Arukh printings expand the library survey; Ramon Martí’s Pugio fidei represents medieval Christian use of rabbinic quotations.
The Pugio’s seventeenth-century editions and influence are linked to Voisin and Carpzov; Lightfoot’s Horae offers another Jewish-context approach.
Lightfoot’s editions and successors connect rabbinic knowledge with New Testament exposition; the survey gives Greifswald shelfmarks for later examples.
The collection includes Billerbeck’s fuller Matthew manuscript and major Wolf/De Rossi bibliographies; Willi notes their sources and historical value.
Fuerst’s bibliography closes that survey; Willi explains written and oral Torah as complementary guidance and application.
Rabbinic interpretation continually applies Torah; this conceptual division organizes the Judaica holdings discussed next.
The library has the Warsaw rabbinic Bible and sixteenth-century Pentateuch printings; a footnote identifies the rabbinic commentary repertoire.
Buxtorf’s Basel rabbinic Bible and masoretic Tiberias represent Christian engagement with textual and interpretive Jewish tradition.
The second Tiberias edition involves four Buxtorfs; Levita’s grammatical works and Jewish aid to Christian Hebrew study are traced.
Levita’s Ibn Ezra edition leads into disputes over Jewish transmission and inspiration involving Buxtorf and Morinus.
Cappel’s textual criticism and conservative responses frame the four major polyglot Bibles and the role of recitation traditions.
Greifswald’s London polyglot, Castell lexicon, critical editions and Spinoza first edition are listed with shelfmarks and printing details.
Michaelis’s Hebrew Bible occurs three times; Danz represents a mediating grammar and Buxtorf’s rabbinic lexicon resumes the survey.
Buxtorf’s 1639 lexicon is described as lexicon and early concordance, with a qualified Christian defence of studying the Talmud.
Peiser’s lexicon and the Danz/Rhenferd/Meuschen collection supply rabbinic contextual studies of baptism, law and New Testament passages.
Willi traces early Jewish-German Bible translations; the 1583 Basel Pentateuch is uncatalogued and lacks a shelfmark.
Later German Jewish translations and Lampronti’s realia dictionary lead into the oral Torah holdings and sixteenth-century Mishnah editions.
Mishnah/Tosefta editions accompany Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmud copies; the Jerusalem first edition has explicitly described missing leaves.
Medieval commentaries and mystical works include Maimonides, Nachmanides, the Bahir, Sohar and Rosenroth, with edition and shelfmark detail.
The survey follows Sephardic and Ashkenazic mysticism into Hasidism and records early Midrash collections.
Halakhic works include Tanna deBe Elijahu, Kuzari and Shulchan Aruch; Manasseh ben Israel introduces modern Jewish hope and resettlement arguments.
Mendelssohn and Hirsch exemplify differing modern Jewish positions; prayer and liturgy holdings anchor the library’s depiction of Jewish practice.
Willi lists liturgical editions and Luther’s first-edition Jewish writings, treating the latter as evidence demanding theological self-examination.
Hoffmann, Cohen and Münk counter antisemitic distortion; Willi concludes with a Christian response to Jewish self-understanding after the Shoah.
The last two lines of Willi’s conclusion call for the collected books’ dialogue to become dialogue between people.
Neumann introduces photography’s nineteenth-century development and the early Oriental work of Maxime Du Camp.
Printing and field photography changed scientific documentation; professional studios and state-supported expeditions are identified in the notes.
Anschütz and Hentschel worked in Palestine; PEF, American Colony, École Biblique and Dalman’s institute developed photographic records.
The core collection derives from 1899–1914 course activity; geographical reach and landscape, architectural, ethnographic motifs are summarized.
Pictures served publications and observation; excavation sites are poorly represented because excavating was outside the institute’s assigned work.
Military aerials entered after Dalman moved to Greifswald; wartime exchanges, Hentschel and Schwöbel’s estate expanded the picture collection.
Neumann reconstructs incompatible historic counts and stresses uncertain provenance; the central picture service moved to Hentschel, who held Schwöbel negatives.
Photographs sustained Dalman’s interrupted research and cartographic work; 1925 picture publications mark a change in reproduction quality.
About 1, 200 Jepsen additions dated 1953–1966 preceded stagnation; old plates remained teaching substitutes under DDR travel restrictions.
Projection heat, aging and bacterial damage threatened plates; Zobel’s 1992 project addressed conservation and incomplete catalogues.
Estimated 7, 000 originals included only about 2, 000 labelled/framed items; Greifswald’s database planned image descriptions, restoration, reproduction and access.
